comparator.name: Mathematics
comparator.sourceNotes: The ordinary Mathematics programme has a 135 EC major and 45 EC of profiling choices. This example includes a modelling course in differential equations. It uses restricted and further mathematics choices to build the recommended preparation in differential equations and numerical mathematics. At least 15 EC of profiling must be at level 2 or 3.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Three complete related-fields programmes pass the evidence, coherence, course-content, pairwise distinctness and feasibility gates. The closest route integrates mathematical methods with algorithms, optimisation, probability and data models. The second uses the explicit climate direction to organise a materially different Earth-system and scientific-data curriculum. The third uses the explicit mathematics-for-economics and financial-mathematics interests to organise a quantitative economics and decision-model route. All pairwise differences exceed 30 EC. The biological/life-science and history-of-mathematics directions remain recorded but are not pursued beyond the maximum of three. None of the accepted curricula is presented as proof-intensive pure Mathematics.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both provide programming for mathematical problem solving; UCR supplies a general Python foundation rather than mathematics-specific research programming.
Both teach introductory calculus. Utrecht teaches linear algebra alongside it.
Both study graphs and trees. UCR focuses on algorithms and data structures, while Utrecht also develops combinatorial counting and discrete proofs.
Both develop matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations; the external component also continues calculus.
Both use computational approximation for equations and integrals and assess numerical error.
Both model systems with differential equations; UCR concentrates on linear systems, transforms and state-space representations rather than the full ODE/PDE modelling course.
Both establish probability; UCR integrates probability distributions with estimation, inference and simulation.
Both develop multivariable calculus. Utrecht emphasises proofs and theoretical results in analysis.
UCR logic courses develop formal reasoning, but no selected course reproduces a dedicated proof-writing foundation.
UCR calculus does not reproduce a cumulative proof-intensive analysis course.
UCR has no abstract algebra course in groups and rings.
This later course develops proof-based multivariable analysis and prepares for differentiable manifolds.
Utrecht gives ordinary differential equations and their theory a dedicated course.
General projects and research methods do not reproduce the target’s dedicated mathematics laboratory.
